Benjamin Netanyahu delivered an inflammatory address to the United Nations on Thursday, decrying what he said was a global anti-Jewish conspiracy and swatting aside criticism of Israel’s war in Gaza, as he faces down international isolation and a fight for political survival in upcoming elections in Israel. Photograph: Eyad Baba/AFP/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen New York City, US Benjamin Netanyahu is seen on a television screen speaking during the UN general assembly in New York City. As planned protests erupted on the streets of the city, Netanyahu took aim at critics of the humanitarian crisis in Gaza , the international media, regional leaders such as Turkey’s Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, the leftwing commentator Hasan Piker and the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, in an address that doubled as a stump speech to ignite his rightwing base for the elections. Photograph: Ryan Murphy/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen US Air Force One with Donald Trump onboard flies over a river en route to JFK airport in New York for the UN general assembly. On the first day of the general assembly, Trump denied that the US was running short of critical munitions (‘we have more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using’), attacked the international criminal court as a ‘rogue organisation’ and claimed once again that he was close to settling the war in Ukraine. Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Washington DC, US President Donald Trump, first lady Melania Trump and the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, react after watching a military demonstration at the White House in Washington. At the start of his summit meeting with Trump , the Chinese president called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid the ‘Thucydides trap ’ that could put the US and China on a military collision course amid rising tensions over artificial intelligence, trade and Taiwan. Photograph: Evan Vucci/Reuters Share View image in fullscreen Tehran, Iran Iranian military forces conduct street parades in Tehran. Iran’s seven-day timetable to reopen the strait of Hormuz and start talks on its nuclear programme has been pitched as a deal that could rapidly extricate Donald Trump from a political crisis but requires the US president to make difficult concessions. Photograph: ATP Images/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Kotelniki, Russia A woman looks at a damaged multi-storey residential building hit by what authorities described as a Ukrainian drone strike in Kotelniki . Kyiv has stepped up its campaign of long-range drone strikes against Russia in recent months, particularly against energy infrastructure, a vital source of the Kremlin’s revenue to fund its war effort. Photograph: Reuters Share View image in fullscreen Kyiv, Ukraine Firefighters work to extinguish a fire at an office building in Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district following a strike by a Russian Geran-5 jet-powered attack drone. Just as Ukraine has developed its drone and missile capability to almost match Russia’s – after its cities were subject at times to hundreds of drone strikes a day – Moscow has transformed its drone arsenal with a jet-powered revolution . Photograph: Kostiantyn Liberov/Libkos/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Kramatorsk, Ukraine A priest and a resident walk at the site of a damaged Orthodox church after a Russian airstrike in Kramatorsk. Russia could launch a limited military attack against a Nato country in the coming months, Danish intelligence said this week, in one of the starkest warnings yet by western security services. Photograph: Francisco Richart/Anadolu/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Kyiv, Ukraine Young residents gather as smoke rises over a warehouse, which was hit by a Russian drone strike in Kyiv. In recent weeks, several European intelligence chiefs have warned that Russia may be preparing more assertive actions to test Nato countries’ commitment to supporting Ukraine, though officials differ over how imminent such a move may be. Photograph: Serhii Korovainyi/Reuters Share View image in fullscreen Mediterranean Sea Sudan, a 24-year-old migrant from South Sudan , looks out to sea as the SOS Mediterranee rescue vessel sails toward Marina di Carrara in Italy. Photograph: Stéphane Mahé/Reuters Share View image in fullscreen Neufchâtel-Hardelot, France Migrants try to board a smuggler’s boat off the beach of Hardelot. The body of a man was found on the beach at Neufchâtel-Hardelot shortly after an attempted departure for England. Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Madrid, Spain Members of the Madrid tenants’ union form a barricade in front of the building where 87-year-old Maricarmen was to be evicted. Police fired rounds of teargas and made repeated baton charges as they tried to open a path for a judicial committee to carry out the eviction order, which was eventually executed. Photograph: Fernando Villar/EPA Share View image in fullscreen Xinzo de Limia, Spain Firefighters attempt to extinguish a forest fire near the hamlet of Baltar. Photograph: Adrian Irago/AFP/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Banjar, Indonesia Firefighters extinguish forest and land fires in Banjar. For months, parts of Indonesia’s Borneo and Sumatra islands have been ablaze . The fires are sometimes lit illegally as a cheap way to clear land for plantations of oil palm, of which Indonesia is the world’s largest producer. Photograph: Muda Sagala/AFP/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Trishuli, Nepal People look at a house, damaged during August’s floods at Trishuli. Nepal’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, scolded world leaders at the UN this week , saying last month’s catastrophic deadly flood was a reminder that climate change keeps hurting people who didn’t cause the crisis. Photograph: Aubrey ISD Texas New elementary school in Texas named after beloved longtime school custodian Marilyn Hampton, who regularly bought supplies for and gave rides to children, was honored at public meeting Ramon Antonio Vargas Thu 29 Oct 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 06.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google US schools are often named after presidents, historical figures and civil rights leaders. And soon joining those ranks is a retired longtime Texas school custodian known for going above and beyond her duties by buying classroom supplies for children in need and helping students with their assignments. That heartwarming story centers on Marilyn Hampton, whose former employer of 39 years – the Aubrey independent school district (AISD) – recently moved to rename its new elementary school No 5 in her honor. The AISD’s tribute, announced at a 21 October governing board meeting recorded on video , brought Hampton to joyful tears and quickly went viral among circles dedicated to promoting uplifting news stories. “I still can’t believe it,” Hampton later told the Dallas-Forth Worth news outlet WFAA . “I haven’t stopped crying.” Before retiring in 2022, Hampton spent 39 years as an AISD custodian. But, as officials would later say, she took on much more than custodial work in her role, assisting students with their classwork; buying and delivering them school supplies if they needed them; and staffing the ticket booth at football games. View image in fullscreen Marilyn Hampton. Photograph: Aubrey ISD Thousands of AISD students, teachers and staff members came to draw inspiration from Hampton’s commitment, according to the district’s superintendent, Shannon Saylor. So the AISD ultimately decided to invite her to its October meeting under the guise of speaking about a particular school-related issue – then Saylor asked her to unroll a red carpet and read what was emblazoned on it in navy blue letters. It said: “Marilyn Hampton Elementary School.” “She may not have the official title of an educator – but she was in every meaningful sense a teacher and educator at heart,” Saylor remarked in reference to the namesake of the new school under construction and scheduled to open in August. An emotional Hampton replied, “Y’all are too good.” Covering her mouth, she continued: “I wasn’t expecting this. Thank y’all. I love all of y’all – always miss y’all.” She then composed herself and gazed at a monitor with an AI rendering of the school and a sign on it bearing her name. “They better keep it clean,” Hampton joked, eliciting loud laughter among those at the meeting. When she reflected on the distinction with WFAA, she wore a new Marilyn Hampton elementary school T-shirt and recounted how she was the only one of eight siblings to graduate high school. She told the station she used to consider herself a failure for not going to college – but in time became “very happy with the way things turned out”. She added: “I just thought, You know, Marilyn? God put you where you are supposed to be.’” Explore more on these topics Texas Schools US education news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
